messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Raj was a 58-year-old South Asian man who had experienced torture during his youth. He had managed to rebuild his life in America, working as a Product Manager for a tech company and raising a family with his wife. However, the memories of his trauma continued to haunt him. One particularly chilling incident involved incomprehensible chatter, sirens, and feelings of dizziness that often triggered vivid flashbacks. Raj’s trauma had left him hyper-vigilant and mistrustful of others. He believed there was something inherently wrong with him that made the event happen and that nothing good could come his way anymore. Raj's negative appraisals led to several maladaptive strategies. His belief in not being able to trust anyone or anything made him avoid stressors at all costs. He often found himself constantly checking his body for signs of danger or injury, even when he knew he was safe. Raj’s mistrust extended to military and police uniforms or weapons, which he avoided as much as possible. The sense that there was something inherently wrong with him also heightened his perception of threat. Even in familiar settings, he would react with alarm if someone touched him unexpectedly. His inability to relax, even when in a safe place, underscored his persistent state of alertness. He frequently woke up during the night to check whether he was still safe, further reinforcing his feelings of mistrust and intrinsic fault. These maladaptive strategies further fueled Raj’s negative appraisals. His constant body monitoring and avoidance behaviors made him feel even more isolated and less capable of trusting others. Every sound or movement that reminded him of sirens or incomprehensible chatter sent waves of panic through his body, reinforcing the notion that nothing good could happen to him. The effects of these symptoms were evident in Raj's daily life as a Product Manager. He found it increasingly difficult to engage with colleagues and often avoided meetings where he might feel vulnerable. His work performance suffered, leading to strained relationships at work and a gradual erosion of his confidence. The constant stress made even small tasks seem overwhelming. Despite his efforts to avoid triggers and maintain control over his environment, Raj’s symptoms continued to escalate. He became so preoccupied with avoiding danger that it began to interfere with his ability to enjoy life or engage in meaningful activities outside of work. His wife noticed the changes in him and expressed concern about his increasing isolation and anxiety. Raj finally sought help after a particularly distressing night where he woke up several times, convinced he was no longer safe. The fear of reliving the trauma and the belief that nothing good could happen to him had become too much to bear. He hoped therapy would provide some relief from the constant vigilance and mistrust that now dominated his life. In seeking help, Raj was most afraid that his fears were justified and that he might never be able to trust others or feel safe again. However, he also harbored a glimmer of hope that with support and understanding, he could regain control over his life and find some peace from the past.
